AEGIS: Anchor-Enforced Gradient Isolation for
Knowledge-Preserving Vision-Language-Action Fine-Tuning

Guransh Singh Affiliation: Independent Researcher Email: guransh766@gmail.com
Abstract

Adapting pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs) for robotic control requires injecting high-magnitude continuous gradients from a flow-matching action expert into a backbone trained exclusively with cross-entropy. This cross-modal gradient asymmetry—the spectral dimensionality mismatch between low-rank MSE regression gradients and the high-dimensional semantic manifold sculpted by CE pre-training, causes rapid, severe erosion of the VLM’s visual-question-answering (VQA) capability. Industry-standard defences either sever the gradient pathway entirely via stop-gradient, discarding the rich continuous supervision, or restrict parameter capacity through low-rank adapters (LoRA) that constrain the rank of updates but not their direction, and thus still overwrite the pre-trained manifold.

We introduce AEGIS (Anchor-Enforced Gradient Isolation System): a buffer-free, layer-wise orthogonal gradient projection framework that enables direct continuous MSE learning while preserving the pre-trained VQA manifold—without any co-training data or replay buffer. AEGIS pre-computes a static Gaussian reference anchor from masked VQA forward passes across all transformer layers, then at each training step constructs a Wasserstein-22 transport penalty that generates an anchor-restoration gradient. A sequential dual-backward decomposes the task and anchor gradients; for each transformer layer, AEGIS applies a single Gram–Schmidt orthogonal projection that bends the task gradient away from the destructive direction while preserving its constructive content. The projection sheds less than 1%1\% of gradient energy on average, yet eliminates the cumulative activation drift that drives severe forgetting.

1 Introduction

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models adapt pre-trained VLMs for robotic control by fine-tuning on action-labelled demonstration data (Brohan et al., 2023; Black et al., 2024). The promise is compelling: a single foundation model that reasons about language commands, understands visual scenes, and produces continuous motor actions. The reality is precarious: the VLM backbone contains billions of parameters whose loss-landscape geometry has been sculpted by trillions of cross-entropy tokens; action fine-tuning injects a qualitatively alien training signal that overwrites these representations destructively.

The cross-modal gradient asymmetry.

A VLM pre-trained with cross-entropy (CE) develops an intricate network of delicate visual-semantic parameters. Conversely, a flow-matching action expert (Black et al., 2024) produces high-magnitude, low-rank MSE gradients targeting a narrow physical subspace. When these high-magnitude MSE gradients backpropagate into the VLM, standard optimisers blast this concentrated robotic update indiscriminately across the network, destructively overwriting the semantic representations. We term this fundamental geometric mismatch cross-modal gradient asymmetry.

In our experiments, naive fine-tuning that allows direct MSE gradient flow causes a significant, steady degradation in VQA holdout loss within 1,5001{,}500 steps (Figure 3), severely eroding the VLM’s pre-trained visual reasoning capability.

The co-training tax.

Current industrial VLA systems employ two workarounds to mitigate this problem, both of which impose substantial costs:

  1. 1.

    Stop-gradient routing (Driess and others, 2025; Black et al., 2024) severs the MSE gradient pathway entirely via sg⁡(⋅)\mathrm{sg}(\cdot), preventing continuous gradients from reaching the VLM backbone. This forces the system to rely on discrete proxy tokens (e.g., FAST (Pertsch et al., 2025)) as the sole VLM learning signal, discarding the rich continuous supervision available in demonstration data. While stop-gradient preserves VQA (our stop-gradient baseline shows VQA loss remaining roughly constant), this preservation comes at the cost of encoding robot actions as discrete tokens in the LLM vocabulary—a representational proxy that compresses continuous 77-DoF motor commands into a foreign code-space.

  2. 2.

    Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) (Hancock et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2022) restricts the capacity of learning by confining weight updates to a low-rank subspace (r=16r{=}16, α=32\alpha{=}32 on LLM layers). However, LoRA does not restrict the geometry of learning: if the MSE gradient projects destructively onto the VQA manifold within the low-rank subspace, LoRA will faithfully execute that destructive update. Our experiments confirm this: our LoRA baseline slows degradation but still causes a steady increase in VQA loss (Figure 3), demonstrating that low-rank constraints alone are insufficient against cross-modal gradient asymmetry.

Critically, both strategies in production systems additionally rely on mixed-batch VQA co-training—interleaving VQA data (up to 50%50\%) into the robotic training batches to artificially maintain the pre-trained distribution (Driess and others, 2025; Hancock et al., 2025). This “co-training tax” doubles the effective compute cost and requires maintaining access to the original VQA corpus during robotic fine-tuning.

AEGIS: gradient surgery on the Wasserstein manifold.

We propose AEGIS (Anchor-Enforced Gradient Isolation System), a framework that resolves the cross-modal gradient asymmetry at its geometric root. AEGIS consists of three components:

  1. 1.

    Static Wasserstein anchor (Section 4.1): Before fine-tuning, AEGIS pre-computes per-layer Gaussian statistics (𝝁ℓ0,𝝈ℓ0 2)(\bm{\mu}^{0}_{\ell},\bm{\sigma}^{0\,2}_{\ell}) from masked VQA forward passes across all 2626 transformer layers of the VLM. These statistics define a reference point on the Wasserstein-22 manifold of activation distributions. The anchor deliberately uses the full attention mask (images ++ text) to capture the complete semantic manifold, while excluding padding tokens to prevent phantom attractors at non-semantic zero-vectors.

  2. 2.

    Wasserstein-22 transport penalty (Section 4.2): At each training step, AEGIS computes the squared 𝒲2\mathcal{W}_{2} distance between the current and anchor activation statistics, decomposed via the Bures metric into mean-shift and standard-deviation-mismatch terms. This penalty generates a second set of gradients through the same computation graph.

  3. 3.

    Layer-wise orthogonal gradient projection (Section 4.3): A sequential dual-backward decomposes the task (FM) and anchor (OT) gradients. For each transformer layer, AEGIS computes a single global projection coefficient αℓ=⟨𝒈taskℓ,𝒈otℓ⟩/‖𝒈otℓ‖2\alpha_{\ell}=\langle{\bm{g}}_{\text{task}}^{\ell},{\bm{g}}_{\text{ot}}^{\ell}\rangle/\|{\bm{g}}_{\text{ot}}^{\ell}\|^{2} and, when destructive (αℓ<0\alpha_{\ell}<0), subtracts the interfering component: 𝒈finalℓ=𝒈taskℓ−αℓ​𝒈otℓ{\bm{g}}_{\text{final}}^{\ell}={\bm{g}}_{\text{task}}^{\ell}-\alpha_{\ell}\,{\bm{g}}_{\text{ot}}^{\ell}. This Gram–Schmidt step bends the task gradient orthogonal to the anchor manifold’s normal direction, preserving all constructive gradient energy while eliminating the destructive projection. The layer-wise granularity—neither global (which suffers from a “zero-sum loophole” where opposing layers cancel) nor per-tensor (which destroys attention-head synchronisation)—is the geometric sweet spot that respects the internal structure of transformer blocks.

AEGIS is purely a backward-pass intervention: the forward pass, loss functions, and model architecture remain entirely unchanged. The VLM sees only action data during training—no VQA co-training, no replay buffer, no discrete proxy tokens.

Contributions.

Our contributions are:

  1. 1.

    We identify cross-modal gradient asymmetry as the root cause of VQA degradation during VLA fine-tuning, demonstrating how highly concentrated MSE gradients overwrite delicate semantic parameters (Section 3).

  2. 2.

    We formalise AEGIS, a buffer-free framework that constructs a Wasserstein-22 Gaussian anchor over the pre-trained activation manifold and performs per-layer Gram–Schmidt orthogonal projection to eliminate destructive gradient interference while preserving constructive task learning (Section 4).

2 Related Work

Vision-Language-Action models.

RT-2 (Brohan et al., 2023) demonstrated that VLMs can directly output tokenised actions. π0\pi_{0} (Black et al., 2024) integrates a flow-matching action expert with a VLM backbone via cross-attention, establishing the hybrid architecture that our work builds upon. OpenVLA (Kim et al., 2024) open-sourced a 7B VLA with discrete action tokenisation. KIVA (Driess and others, 2025) introduced the stop-gradient operator to prevent flow-matching gradients from corrupting VLM weights, enabling use of the FAST tokeniser (Pertsch et al., 2025) for discrete action representation. Concurrently, VLM2VLA (Hancock et al., 2025) identifies action gradients as destructive and proposes LoRA fine-tuning on the VLM’s LLM layers. Our LoRA baseline directly replicates the VLM2VLA configuration and shows that it fails to prevent VQA erosion, as destructive MSE gradient components persist and overwrite the VQA manifold even within the low-rank subspace. AEGIS is complementary to both: it operates on gradient geometry rather than data representation or parameter capacity, and can in principle be combined with LoRA or discrete tokenisation.

Catastrophic forgetting and regularisation-based defences.

EWC (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017) penalises changes to Fisher-important parameters via a quadratic loss-level regulariser: ℒEWC=ℒtask+λ2​∑iFi​(θi−θi∗)2\mathcal{L}_{\text{EWC}}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{task}}+\frac{\lambda}{2}\sum_{i}F_{i}(\theta_{i}-\theta_{i}^{*})^{2}. Synaptic Intelligence (Zenke et al., 2017) accumulates online importance scores. All regularisation methods model knowledge preservation as a static Euclidean penalty basin: the quadratic restoring force scales linearly with parameter displacement |θi−θi∗||\theta_{i}-\theta_{i}^{*}| and is therefore overwhelmed in early training when θ≈θ∗\theta\approx\theta^{*}, exactly the regime where cross-modal gradient shock is most violent. AEGIS differs fundamentally: it detects and removes destructive gradient components before they reach the optimiser, leaving the forward pass and loss function unchanged.

Orthogonal gradient projection (OGP).

OGD (Farajtabar et al., 2020) projects onto the orthogonal complement of previous task gradients stored in memory. A-GEM (Chaudhry et al., 2019) maintains a replay buffer of past task data and constrains new gradients to not increase the replayed loss. GPM (Saha et al., 2021) constructs orthogonal projectors from gradient subspace bases of previous tasks. All existing OGP methods require either (i) explicit replay buffers storing raw data or gradient bases from previous tasks, or (ii) per-step gradient computations on the reference task. AEGIS introduces a novel OGP formulation that constructs the projection reference from a statistical manifold anchor—pre-computed Gaussian activation statistics—requiring no replay buffer, no reference-task data access during training, and no per-step reference gradient computation. The projection reference is derived from the Wasserstein-22 geometry of the anchor distribution, not from raw gradient memories.

Gradient surgery.

PCGrad (Yu et al., 2020) projects conflicting multi-task gradients. GradDrop (Chen et al., 2020) randomly drops gradient components with conflicting signs. Both operate in flat Euclidean space: they treat every parameter dimension equally, ignoring the curved geometry of the loss landscape. AEGIS projects onto a geometrically meaningful reference direction derived from the Wasserstein manifold of activation statistics, and operates at the layer granularity rather than the parameter or global level—a critical design choice that we ablate in Section 4.3.

Activation-level regularisation.

Knowledge distillation (Hinton et al., 2015) constrains student activations to match a teacher but requires maintaining a full teacher model during training. Feature-level alignment methods penalise drift in intermediate representations. AEGIS draws from optimal transport theory: it computes a Wasserstein-22 penalty between current and pre-trained activation statistics via the closed-form Bures metric for diagonal-covariance Gaussians (Dowson and Landau, 1982), yielding a geometrically interpretable anchor that requires only pre-computed first- and second-order statistics—not a live teacher. Unlike KL divergence, 𝒲2\mathcal{W}_{2} remains bounded as σit→0\sigma^{t}_{i}\to 0, providing smooth, well-conditioned gradients throughout training.

3 Problem Formalisation

3.1 Setup

Consider a VLM with parameters 𝜽∈ℝd{\bm{\theta}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, pre-trained on a distribution 𝒟VLM\mathcal{D}_{\text{VLM}} (e.g., image-text pairs for VQA). We fine-tune 𝜽{\bm{\theta}} on a robotic action-prediction task with distribution 𝒟action\mathcal{D}_{\text{action}}, using a flow-matching (FM) action expert ϕ\bm{\phi} (Lipman et al., 2023; Black et al., 2024) that cross-attends to the VLM’s hidden states:

ℒFM​(𝜽,ϕ)=𝔼t,ϵ​[‖𝒗ϕ​(𝒂t,𝒉𝜽,t)−(𝒂1−ϵ)‖22],\mathcal{L}_{\text{FM}}({\bm{\theta}},\bm{\phi})=\mathbb{E}_{t,\bm{\epsilon}}\left[\left\|\bm{v}_{\bm{\phi}}\!\left(\bm{a}_{t};\bm{h}_{\bm{\theta}},t\right)-(\bm{a}_{1}-\bm{\epsilon})\right\|^{2}_{2}\right], (1)

where 𝒂t=t​𝒂1+(1−t)​ϵ\bm{a}_{t}=t\bm{a}_{1}+(1-t)\bm{\epsilon} is the noisy action at time t∼Beta​(1.5,1.0)t\sim\text{Beta}(1.5,1.0), ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\bm{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), and 𝒉𝜽\bm{h}_{\bm{\theta}} are the VLM’s last-layer hidden states. The expert 𝒗ϕ\bm{v}_{\bm{\phi}} predicts the velocity field of a continuous normalising flow over 5050-step, 77-DoF action trajectories.

3.2 Cross-Modal Gradient Asymmetry

The VLM’s parameter landscape has been shaped by softmax-normalised log-probability gradients from cross-entropy training. These gradients possess a broad, high-dimensional spectral signature, distributing energy across many singular directions to encode complex, delicate semantic relationships. By contrast, the continuous MSE loss of flow-matching generates gradients with a fundamentally narrow, low-rank spectral profile, concentrating energy into a small number of dominant physical-action directions.

Definition 3.1 (Spectral Profile).

For a loss ℒ\mathcal{L} and layer parameters 𝛉ℓ{\bm{\theta}}_{\ell}, define the gradient singular-value spectrum as the ordered singular values σ1≥σ2≥⋯≥σr\sigma_{1}\geq\sigma_{2}\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_{r} of the gradient tensor ∇𝛉ℓℒ\nabla_{{\bm{\theta}}_{\ell}}\mathcal{L} reshaped as a matrix. The spectral concentration ratio is:

κk=∑i=1kσi2∑i=1rσi2,\kappa_{k}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sigma_{i}^{2}}{\sum_{i=1}^{r}\sigma_{i}^{2}}, (2)

measuring the fraction of gradient energy in the top-kk directions.

Definition 3.2 (Cross-Modal Gradient Asymmetry).

Cross-modal gradient asymmetry occurs when the task gradient 𝐠FM=∇𝛉ℒFM{\bm{g}}_{\text{FM}}=\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{FM}} has a spectral profile that is misaligned with the VLM’s pre-trained gradient geometry. Specifically, the CE-trained VLM distributes its energy broadly across hundreds of dimensions (κ20CE≪0.9\kappa_{20}^{\text{CE}}\ll 0.9), while the MSE task gradient is highly concentrated (κ20MSE>0.9\kappa_{20}^{\text{MSE}}>0.9), possessing a narrow, high-magnitude physical subspace.

The destructive mechanism is as follows. Let 𝑯ℓt∈ℝB×S×dℓ\bm{H}_{\ell}^{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times S\times d_{\ell}} denote the hidden-state tensor at layer ℓ\ell after tt gradient steps. Standard optimisers take the narrow, high-magnitude MSE gradient and blast it across the network. Because this update is spectrally top-heavy and physically rigid, the resulting parameter perturbation Δ​𝜽t=𝜽t−𝜽0\Delta{\bm{\theta}}^{t}={\bm{\theta}}^{t}-{\bm{\theta}}^{0} indiscriminately overwrites the fine-grained, delicate semantic weights distributed across the broader singular dimensions. This causes the activation distribution p⁡(𝑯ℓt)p(\bm{H}_{\ell}^{t}) to drift away from the pre-trained distribution p⁡(𝑯ℓ0)p(\bm{H}_{\ell}^{0}), destroying the geometric priors that enable visual question answering.

3.3 Why Existing Defences Fail

Stop-gradient (sg\mathrm{sg}).

Setting ∇𝜽ℒFM=𝟎\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{FM}}=\mathbf{0} eliminates the cross-modal gradient entirely. This preserves VQA (our stop-gradient baseline confirms VQA loss remaining roughly constant), but it discards the dense continuous supervision available in demonstration data, forcing reliance on discrete proxy tokens (FAST) as the sole VLM learning signal. The VLM never learns from the 50×7=35050\times 7=350-dimensional continuous action manifold—the richest supervisory signal in the dataset.

Low-rank adaptation (LoRA).

While LoRA constrains weight updates to a low-rank subspace (Δ​W=B​A\Delta W=BA), this generic subspace is rarely aligned with the delicate VQA-critical parameter directions. Consequently, any destructive cross-modal gradients cleanly projecting into this subspace are still faithfully executed. Our baseline confirms that LoRA slows, but cannot prevent, the steady increase in VQA loss.

EWC and loss-level penalties.

EWC (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017) adds a quadratic penalty λ2​∑iFi​(θi−θi∗)2\frac{\lambda}{2}\sum_{i}F_{i}(\theta_{i}-\theta^{*}_{i})^{2} producing a restoring force that scales linearly with displacement. Under cross-modal gradient shock, |gi|≫λ​Fi​|θi−θi∗||g_{i}|\gg\lambda F_{i}|\theta_{i}-\theta_{i}^{*}| in early training: the penalty is overwhelmed before it activates.

The AEGIS principle.

Rather than constraining the magnitude of updates (LoRA), the loss surface (EWC), or severing the gradient (stop-gradient), AEGIS operates on the direction of the gradient: it identifies and removes only the destructive projection of the task gradient onto the anchor manifold’s normal direction, preserving all constructive gradient energy.

4 Method: AEGIS

AEGIS consists of three components: (i) a static Wasserstein anchor computed before training, (ii) a per-step Wasserstein-22 transport penalty computed from the same forward pass as the task loss, and (iii) a layer-wise orthogonal gradient projection that eliminates destructive interference while preserving constructive learning. All three are implemented as backward-pass interventions: the forward pass and loss functions remain unchanged.

4.1 Static Wasserstein Anchor

The AEGIS pipeline begins by establishing a geometric reference point—the activation statistics of the pre-trained VLM on its native distribution—before any fine-tuning occurs.

Full-sequence masked aggregation.

Padding tokens carry no semantic content; including them would create a phantom attractor at non-semantic zero-vectors, adding systematic bias. We define the set of valid positions via the attention mask 𝑴∈{0,1}B×S\bm{M}\in\{0,1\}^{B\times S}, where BB is batch size and SS the sequence length. AEGIS computes anchor statistics using the full attention mask covering both image tokens and text tokens. The rationale is that the orthogonal projection operates at the gradient level, not the activation level: the anchor defines a reference direction for gradient interference detection, and using the full semantic content of the VQA manifold (including the generative answer tokens) provides a more complete reference geometry. For layer ℓ\ell with hidden-state tensor 𝑯ℓ∈ℝB×S×dℓ\bm{H}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times S\times d_{\ell}}, the masked mean and variance are:

𝝁ℓ0=∑n,sMn,s⋅𝒉ℓ(n,s)C,𝝈ℓ0 2=∑n,sMn,s⋅(𝒉ℓ(n,s)−𝝁ℓ0)2C,C=∑n,sMn,s.\bm{\mu}^{0}_{\ell}=\frac{\sum_{n,s}M_{n,s}\cdot\bm{h}^{(n,s)}_{\ell}}{C},\quad\bm{\sigma}^{0\,2}_{\ell}=\frac{\sum_{n,s}M_{n,s}\cdot(\bm{h}^{(n,s)}_{\ell}-\bm{\mu}^{0}_{\ell})^{2}}{C},\quad C=\sum_{n,s}M_{n,s}. (3)
All-layer coverage.

AEGIS registers forward hooks at all L=26L=26 transformer layers of the VLM’s language model. This ensures that the orthogonal projection can detect and correct gradient interference at every depth of the network—from early layers encoding low-level visual features to late layers encoding high-level linguistic reasoning.

Online accumulation.

Rather than storing all hidden states, we register forward hooks that accumulate per-batch (𝝁batch,𝝈batch2)(\bm{\mu}_{\text{batch}},\bm{\sigma}^{2}_{\text{batch}}) via running sums. The final anchor {(𝝁ℓ0,𝝈ℓ0 2)}ℓ=0L−1\{(\bm{\mu}^{0}_{\ell},\bm{\sigma}^{0\,2}_{\ell})\}_{\ell=0}^{L-1} is the batch-averaged expectation:

𝝁ℓ0=1Nbatches​∑j=1Nbatches𝝁ℓ,j,𝝈ℓ0 2=1Nbatches​∑j=1Nbatches𝝈ℓ,j2.\bm{\mu}^{0}_{\ell}=\frac{1}{N_{\text{batches}}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{\text{batches}}}\bm{\mu}_{\ell,j},\qquad\bm{\sigma}^{0\,2}_{\ell}=\frac{1}{N_{\text{batches}}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{\text{batches}}}\bm{\sigma}^{2}_{\ell,j}. (4)

The complete anchor is saved as a static .pt file—a one-time cost of ∼5{\sim}5 minutes on a single GPU for 3,0003{,}000 VQA v2 samples.

4.2 Wasserstein-22 Transport Penalty

At each training step, the VLM processes a robotic action batch and produces hidden-state tensors across all layers. AEGIS computes the current activation statistics using the same masked aggregation as the anchor:

𝝁ℓt=(𝑯ℓt⊙𝑴exp)⋅𝟏Ct,𝝈ℓt​ 2=((𝑯ℓt−𝝁ℓt)2⊙𝑴exp)⋅𝟏Ct,\bm{\mu}^{t}_{\ell}=\frac{(\bm{H}^{t}_{\ell}\odot\bm{M}_{\text{exp}})\cdot\mathbf{1}}{C^{t}},\qquad\bm{\sigma}^{t\,2}_{\ell}=\frac{((\bm{H}^{t}_{\ell}-\bm{\mu}^{t}_{\ell})^{2}\odot\bm{M}_{\text{exp}})\cdot\mathbf{1}}{C^{t}}, (5)

where Ct=∑MtC^{t}=\sum M^{t} counts valid positions in the current batch. The use of identical masked reduction in both anchor and online statistics is critical: it ensures that the transport cost measures semantic manifold displacement rather than artefacts from variable-length padding.

Bures metric decomposition.

For diagonal-covariance Gaussians 𝒩⁡(𝝁0,diag⁡(𝝈0 2))\mathcal{N}(\bm{\mu}^{0},\mathrm{diag}(\bm{\sigma}^{0\,2})) and 𝒩⁡(𝝁t,diag⁡(𝝈t​ 2))\mathcal{N}(\bm{\mu}^{t},\mathrm{diag}(\bm{\sigma}^{t\,2})), the squared Wasserstein-22 distance admits the closed-form Bures metric (Dowson and Landau, 1982):

𝒲22​(𝒩ℓ0,𝒩ℓt)=‖𝝁ℓt−𝝁ℓ0‖22⏟mean shift+‖𝝈ℓt​ 2+ϵ−𝝈ℓ0 2+ϵ‖22⏟std mismatch (Bures),\mathcal{W}_{2}^{2}(\mathcal{N}^{0}_{\ell},\mathcal{N}^{t}_{\ell})=\underbrace{\left\|\bm{\mu}^{t}_{\ell}-\bm{\mu}^{0}_{\ell}\right\|^{2}_{2}}_{\text{mean shift}}+\underbrace{\left\|\sqrt{\bm{\sigma}^{t\,2}_{\ell}+\epsilon}-\sqrt{\bm{\sigma}^{0\,2}_{\ell}+\epsilon}\right\|^{2}_{2}}_{\text{std mismatch (Bures)}}, (6)

where ϵ=10−6\epsilon=10^{-6} ensures numerical stability. Note: In our implementation, we compute the mean squared error rather than the sum to normalize across varying hidden dimensions dd, effectively scaling 𝒲22\mathcal{W}_{2}^{2} by 1/d1/d to ensure gradient magnitude stability.

The total AEGIS transport penalty sums over all L=26L=26 layers:

ℒOT=∑ℓ=0L−1𝒲22​(𝒩ℓ0,𝒩ℓt).\mathcal{L}_{\text{OT}}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{L-1}\mathcal{W}_{2}^{2}(\mathcal{N}^{0}_{\ell},\mathcal{N}^{t}_{\ell}). (7)
Why 𝒲2\mathcal{W}_{2} and not KL?

The KL divergence KL(𝒩t∥𝒩0)\mathrm{KL}(\mathcal{N}^{t}\|\mathcal{N}^{0}) is unbounded as σit→0\sigma^{t}_{i}\to 0, creating gradient explosions near collapsed dimensions—a common failure mode during aggressive fine-tuning. 𝒲2\mathcal{W}_{2} remains bounded and provides a smooth metric on the space of distributions, yielding well-conditioned gradients throughout training. The Bures decomposition separates location drift (mean shift) from shape distortion (std mismatch), giving AEGIS independent geometric control over both forms of activation corruption.

Role of ℒOT\mathcal{L}_{\text{OT}} in AEGIS.

Crucially, ℒOT\mathcal{L}_{\text{OT}} is not added to the task loss. It is used only to generate a reference gradient direction 𝒈ot=∇𝜽ℒOT{\bm{g}}_{\text{ot}}=\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{OT}} via a second backward pass. This gradient encodes the direction in parameter space that would restore the activation statistics to the pre-trained anchor. AEGIS uses this direction as the reference for orthogonal projection, not as a loss-level regulariser.

4.3 Layer-Wise Orthogonal Gradient Projection

The central algorithmic contribution of AEGIS is its layer-wise orthogonal gradient projection (OGP), which decomposes the task and anchor gradients via a sequential dual-backward and applies Gram–Schmidt orthogonalisation at the transformer-layer granularity.

4.3.1 Sequential Dual-Backward

The task loss ℒFM\mathcal{L}_{\text{FM}} and anchor penalty ℒOT\mathcal{L}_{\text{OT}} share the same computation graph (both depend on the VLM’s hidden states 𝑯t\bm{H}^{t}). Rather than adding them as ℒFM+λ​ℒOT\mathcal{L}_{\text{FM}}+\lambda\mathcal{L}_{\text{OT}} (which would conflate their gradient signals with a scalar tradeoff), AEGIS decomposes the backward pass into two stages:

Stage 1: Task gradient extraction.

Backpropagate ℒFM\mathcal{L}_{\text{FM}} with graph retention:

𝒈task=∇𝜽ℒFM​(𝜽,ϕ),retain_graph=True.{\bm{g}}_{\text{task}}=\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{FM}}({\bm{\theta}},\bm{\phi}),\qquad\text{retain\_graph=True}. (8)

For each trainable VLM parameter, cache the task gradient and zero the gradient buffer.

Stage 2: OT gradient extraction.

Backpropagate ℒOT\mathcal{L}_{\text{OT}} through the same computation graph:

𝒈ot=∇𝜽ℒOT​(𝜽).{\bm{g}}_{\text{ot}}=\nabla_{\bm{\theta}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{OT}}({\bm{\theta}}). (9)

For each trainable VLM parameter, cache the OT gradient and zero the gradient buffer.

4.3.2 Layer-Wise Gram–Schmidt Projection

After extracting both gradient vectors, AEGIS groups VLM parameters by transformer layer. Parameters belonging to transformer layer ℓ\ell (all weight matrices within that layer: qq-, kk-, vv-, oo-projections, up/down/gate MLPs, layer norms) are treated as a single geometric entity.

Step A: Compute layer-level geometry.

For each layer group ℓ\ell, flatten and concatenate all parameter gradients to obtain the layer-level task and OT gradient vectors:

𝒈taskℓ=⨁p∈Θℓvec​(𝒈task,p),𝒈otℓ=⨁p∈Θℓvec​(𝒈ot,p).{\bm{g}}_{\text{task}}^{\ell}=\bigoplus_{p\in\Theta_{\ell}}\text{vec}({\bm{g}}_{\text{task},p}),\qquad{\bm{g}}_{\text{ot}}^{\ell}=\bigoplus_{p\in\Theta_{\ell}}\text{vec}({\bm{g}}_{\text{ot},p}). (10)

Compute the raw dot product and norms:

dℓ=⟨𝒈taskℓ,𝒈otℓ⟩,cos⁡θℓ=dℓ‖𝒈taskℓ‖⋅‖𝒈otℓ‖+ϵ.d_{\ell}=\langle{\bm{g}}_{\text{task}}^{\ell},{\bm{g}}_{\text{ot}}^{\ell}\rangle,\quad\cos\theta_{\ell}=\frac{d_{\ell}}{\|{\bm{g}}_{\text{task}}^{\ell}\|\cdot\|{\bm{g}}_{\text{ot}}^{\ell}\|+\epsilon}. (11)
Step B: Detect destructive interference.

The sign of dℓd_{\ell} partitions each layer into one of two regimes:

  • •

    dℓ≥0d_{\ell}\geq 0 (constructive alignment): The task gradient does not conflict with the anchor restoration direction. The gradient passes through unmodified: 𝒈finalℓ=𝒈taskℓ{\bm{g}}_{\text{final}}^{\ell}={\bm{g}}_{\text{task}}^{\ell}.

  • •

    dℓ<0d_{\ell}<0 (destructive interference): The task gradient has a component that pushes activations away from the pre-trained anchor. AEGIS computes the projection coefficient:

    αℓ=dℓ‖𝒈otℓ‖2+ϵ,αℓ<0.\alpha_{\ell}=\frac{d_{\ell}}{\|{\bm{g}}_{\text{ot}}^{\ell}\|^{2}+\epsilon},\qquad\alpha_{\ell}<0. (12)
Step C: Gram–Schmidt orthogonal subtraction.

When αℓ<0\alpha_{\ell}<0, the interfering component is subtracted:

𝒈finalℓ=𝒈taskℓ−αℓ​𝒈otℓ.{\bm{g}}_{\text{final}}^{\ell}={\bm{g}}_{\text{task}}^{\ell}-\alpha_{\ell}\,{\bm{g}}_{\text{ot}}^{\ell}. (13)

Since αℓ<0\alpha_{\ell}<0, the subtraction adds a component in the 𝒈otℓ{\bm{g}}_{\text{ot}}^{\ell} direction, bending the task gradient away from the destructive direction and toward (or past) the orthogonal complement of 𝒈otℓ{\bm{g}}_{\text{ot}}^{\ell}. The resulting gradient 𝒈finalℓ{\bm{g}}_{\text{final}}^{\ell} satisfies:

⟨𝒈finalℓ,𝒈otℓ⟩=0,\langle{\bm{g}}_{\text{final}}^{\ell},{\bm{g}}_{\text{ot}}^{\ell}\rangle=0, (14)

i.e., the final gradient is exactly orthogonal to the anchor restoration direction.

Remark 4.1 (Why layer-wise?).

Three granularity levels are natural choices for gradient projection:

  1. 1.

    Global (model-level): Compute a single projection coefficient for the entire VLM. This suffers from the “zero-sum loophole”: destructive interference in one layer can be masked by constructive alignment in another, causing the global dd to appear benign while individual layers are devastated.

  2. 2.

    Per-tensor: Compute a separate projection for every weight matrix. This destroys the synchronisation of attention heads within a layer: the qq-, kk-, vv-, and oo-projections are geometrically coupled, and independently projecting their gradients can cause “logit smearing”—a de-synchronisation of attention patterns that manifests as diffuse, unfocused attention.

  3. 3.

    Layer-wise (AEGIS): Treat each transformer layer as an atomic geometric entity. This preserves the internal coupling of attention heads while independently resolving interference at each depth of the network.

Our experiments confirm that layer-wise granularity achieves the best VQA preservation.

Geometric Properties.

By the definition of Gram–Schmidt orthogonalisation, the resulting gradient is strictly orthogonal to the anchor restoration direction (⟨𝒈finalℓ,𝒈otℓ⟩=0\langle{\bm{g}}_{\text{final}}^{\ell},{\bm{g}}_{\text{ot}}^{\ell}\rangle=0). Furthermore, applying the Pythagorean theorem to this decomposition guarantees that the projected gradient preserves energy proportional to its alignment: ‖𝒈finalℓ‖2=‖𝒈taskℓ‖2​(1−cos2⁡θℓ)\|{\bm{g}}_{\text{final}}^{\ell}\|^{2}=\|{\bm{g}}_{\text{task}}^{\ell}\|^{2}(1-\cos^{2}\theta_{\ell}). This ensures that AEGIS enforces its geometric constraint with minimal intervention: even at mild conflict (e.g., |cos⁡θℓ|≈0.1|\cos\theta_{\ell}|\approx 0.1), the gradient safely retains 99%99\% of its constructive energy.

Remark 4.2 (Comparison with PCGrad).

PCGrad (Yu et al., 2020) performs an analogous projection but operates at the global level with respect to a simultaneously computed conflicting task gradient. AEGIS differs in three critical ways: (i) the projection reference is derived from a statistical manifold anchor (Wasserstein geometry), not from a competing task; (ii) the projection is applied at the layer granularity; (iii) no second task exists—the “conflict” is between the task gradient and the manifold-restoration direction, making AEGIS a single-task method with a geometric constraint.

5 Experimental Setup

5.1 Model and Data

We use PaliGemma2-3B-Mix-224 (Beyer et al., 2024) as our VLM backbone: a SigLIP-400M vision encoder (Zhai et al., 2023) (frozen in all conditions) paired with a Gemma-2B language model (Team, 2024) and a multi-modal projector (both trainable). Action data comes from LIBERO (Liu et al., 2024), a benchmark suite of tabletop manipulation tasks. We combine all task suites into a single HDF5 dataset. Each sample consists of two RGB images (agent view + wrist camera), proprioceptive state (joint positions and gripper state), a language instruction, and a 5050-step action horizon of 77-DoF motor commands normalised to [−1,1][-1,1].

Action expert architecture.

All conditions use an identical CrossAttentionFlowExpert: a 44-layer transformer decoder (10241024-dimensional, 88 heads) with sinusoidal time embedding, positional encoding, and a linear output projection to 77-DoF. The expert cross-attends to the VLM’s last-layer hidden states through a learned 2048→10242048\to 1024 projection. Flow-matching noise is sampled as t∼Beta​(1.5,1.0)t\sim\text{Beta}(1.5,1.0), ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\bm{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), with target flow 𝒂1−ϵ\bm{a}_{1}-\bm{\epsilon} and training loss scaled by 10×10\times. All FM losses reported in this paper are unscaled raw MSE (i.e. the training loss divided by 1010).

5.2 VQA Evaluation Protocol

We measure knowledge erosion via a fixed evaluation set of 100100 VQA v2 samples (Goyal et al., 2019), cached before training, evaluated every 2020 steps using the VLM’s native cross-entropy loss on the ground-truth answer tokens. All four conditions share the identical evaluation cache (ℒVQA0≈0.392\mathcal{L}^{0}_{\text{VQA}}\approx 0.392), ensuring direct comparability. The VQA holdout loss ℒVQA\mathcal{L}_{\text{VQA}} provides a continuous, high-resolution measure of forgetting dynamics across the full training trajectory.

5.3 Experimental Conditions

All conditions share identical hyperparameters unless otherwise stated: per-device batch size 44, gradient accumulation 2×2\times (effective batch 88), BF16 mixed precision, gradient clipping at norm 1.01.0, 1,5001{,}500 total steps, no weight decay, no VQA co-training. The VLM sees only robotic action data during training.

  • •

    Naive Fine-Tuning (unshielded baseline): Full-parameter fine-tuning (LLM + projector + flow-matching expert) with unrestricted gradient flow from the MSE loss directly into the VLM backbone. VLM learning rate 2×10−52\times 10^{-5}; expert learning rate 1×10−41\times 10^{-4}; constant schedule with 100100-step warmup. No discrete action head. This represents the worst-case scenario where cross-modal gradient asymmetry operates without any protection.

  • •

    Stop-Gradient + FAST Discrete (industry baseline): Replicates the π0\pi_{0}/KIVA architecture (Black et al., 2024; Driess and others, 2025). The VLM’s hidden states are .detach()’d before entering the action expert, severing the FM gradient pathway. A FAST discrete tokeniser (Pertsch et al., 2025) maps actions to discrete tokens for autoregress ive cross-entropy prediction by the VLM. VLM learning rate 5×10−65\times 10^{-6}; 11 1 The stop-gradient condition uses a reduced VLM LR (5×10−65\times 10^{-6} vs. 2×10−52\times 10^{-5}) following industrial practice for discrete-token VLAs, which are known to require lower LRs to prevent embedding-layer instability from foreign action tokens. This is a favourable setup for the baseline.

  • •

    LoRA Fine-Tuning (PEFT baseline, VLM2VLA-style): Low-rank adaptation (r=16r{=}16, α=32\alpha{=}32) applied via regex to all attention and MLP projections in the language model (q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj, up_proj, down_proj, gate_proj). Base VLM weights are frozen; only LoRA adapters, the multi-modal projector, and the action expert are trainable. VLM learning rate 2×10−52\times 10^{-5}; unrestricted continuous gradient flow (no stop-gradient, no discrete head). This replicates the VLM2VLA configuration (Hancock et al., 2025).

  • •

    AEGIS (ours): Full-parameter fine-tuning of LLM + projector with direct continuous gradient flow from the flow-matching expert (no stop-gradient, no discrete head). Layer-wise orthogonal gradient projection against the Wasserstein-22 anchor, computed over all 2626 transformer layers with the full-sequence mask. VLM learning rate 2×10−52\times 10^{-5}; gradient checkpointing enabled; OT penalty scaled 1×1\times. EMA on the expert (β=0.9999\beta=0.9999).

Design rationale: no co-training.

We deliberately set weight decay to zero for all trainable parameters and do not mix VQA data into any training batch. The model sees only robotic action data, with no implicit or explicit regularisation beyond the method being tested. This creates the most adversarial setting for knowledge preservation and allows clean causal attribution of results: any VQA preservation must arise from the method itself, not from data-level regularisation.

Pre-computation costs.

The static Wasserstein anchor {(𝝁ℓ0,𝝈ℓ0 2)}ℓ=025\{(\bm{\mu}^{0}_{\ell},\bm{\sigma}^{0\,2}_{\ell})\}_{\ell=0}^{25} is computed from 3,0003{,}000 VQA v2 samples via forward hooks on the pre-trained VLM, requiring ∼5{\sim}5 minutes on a single GPU. The resulting tensor is stored as a .pt file and reused across all training runs.

6 Results

6.1 The Spectral Dimensionality Mismatch

Before presenting the comparative results, we provide empirical evidence for the cross-modal gradient asymmetry that motivates AEGIS. Figure 1 plots the singular-value spectrum of real gradients extracted from layers of PaliGemma2-3B-Mix-224 on (i) VQA cross-entropy and (ii) robotic MSE objectives.

The CE gradient distributes energy across hundreds of singular dimensions—a reflection of the high-dimensional semantic manifold required for 257,000257{,}000-class token prediction over a massive vocabulary. In contrast, the MSE gradient collapses within the first ∼20{\sim}20 singular values, concentrating energy in the narrow subspace corresponding to 77-DoF physical regression. Standard SGD/Adam optimisers are blind to this spectral structure: they indiscriminately apply the narrow, high-magnitude MSE gradients across the entire network, forcefully dragging parameters out of their delicate semantic alignment. This spectral dimensionality mismatch is precisely why AEGIS’s orthogonal gradient projection is effective: because the robotic task lives in a much lower-dimensional subspace than VQA, AEGIS can identify the narrow physical gradients and project them orthogonally away from the massive semantic manifold.

6.2 Manifold Preservation

Figure 2 provides direct visual evidence of AEGIS’s manifold-preservation effect by projecting the last-layer hidden states of three model variants (pre-trained baseline, naive fine-tuning, and AEGIS) onto the catastrophic-drift plane.

Naive fine-tuning causes the activation manifold to drift dramatically along the manifold-drift axis, collapsing to a degenerate cluster far from the pre-trained distribution. AEGIS, by contrast, preserves the spatial structure and overlap with the reference manifold—visual confirmation that the orthogonal projection successfully tethers the model’s internal representations to their pre-trained geometry.

6.3 VQA Preservation Under Continuous Fine-Tuning

Figure 3 reveals the longitudinal forgetting dynamics across the four experimental conditions:

  • •

    Naive fine-tuning: Immediate onset of severe forgetting. VQA loss rises sharply from step 00, crossing 0.50.5 by step 300300 and reaching 0.7760.776 by step 1,5001{,}500 (+0.384+0.384), with no sign of stabilisation—the model is still deteriorating at termination (McCloskey and Cohen, 1989).

  • •

    LoRA fine-tuning: Delayed but steady erosion. VQA remains near baseline for ∼200{\sim}200 steps, then rises steadily. The low-rank constraint slows the rate of forgetting but cannot prevent it—consistent with our analysis that LoRA restricts capacity but not gradient geometry. This directly contradicts the premise of VLM2VLA (Hancock et al., 2025), which assumes that LoRA inherently preserves VLM capabilities.

  • •

    AEGIS: Near-complete preservation. VQA loss remains close to baseline throughout training—an order of magnitude less degradation than LoRA and two orders smaller than naive fine-tuning. The VQA trajectory shows that AEGIS successfully isolates the pre-trained semantic manifold from the MSE gradient pressure while allowing the action task to learn through the orthogonal complement.

  • •

    Stop-gradient + FAST: Flat-to-decreasing. VQA loss remains essentially constant or slightly decreasing throughout, as the VLM receives no continuous gradient pressure. However, this preservation comes at the cost of discarding the entire continuous action supervision.

6.4 Action Learning Convergence

Figure 4 confirms that all conditions converge on the continuous FM objective. AEGIS and Naive fine-tuning maintain the fastest action expert convergence, as AEGIS closely tracks the Naive trajectory throughout the entire training run. Naive fine-tuning asymptotically achieves the lowest raw MSE as expected from unrestricted gradient flow. The stop-gradient condition produces the highest FM loss because the VLM never adapts to improve the expert’s conditioning signal.

6.5 Out-of-Distribution OK-VQA Evaluation

To validate that AEGIS’s preservation effect extends beyond the holdout CE loss to actual VQA accuracy, we evaluate all conditions out-of-distribution (OOD) on a 55k evaluation subset of the OK-VQA benchmark (Marino et al., 2019) after training. Table 1 reports the official VQA accuracy scores on this subset.

AEGIS achieves the highest post-training VQA score (60.23%60.23\%), matching the pre-trained baseline (60.15%60.15\%) within statistical noise. Naive fine-tuning drops to 57.36%57.36\% (−2.79-2.79 points absolute), and LoRA degrades to 59.32%59.32\% (−0.83-0.83 points). These results confirm that AEGIS’s geometric intervention preserves the pre-trained VQA manifold as measured by actual question-answering accuracy, not just surrogate CE loss.

6.6 AEGIS Projection Dynamics

AEGIS’s architecture enables full diagnostic visibility into the gradient intervention. We analyse the per-step projection statistics to understand
emphhow much gradient energy AEGIS sheds,
emphhow often it intervenes, and what these dynamics reveal about the geometry of cross-modal interference.

Throttle rate and interference prevalence.

The fraction of transformer layers experiencing destructive interference (Figure 5, top-left) averages 51.2%51.2\% over the full run, with high per-step variance (3.6%3.6\%–100%100\%). This reveals that destructive interference is pervasive but not universal: roughly half of all layers are in conflict at any given step, and which layers conflict varies across batches—a phenomenon invisible to global or per-parameter methods.

Energy shed: surgical precision.

The energy shed (Figure 5, top-right)—the percentage of gradient ℓ2\ell_{2} norm removed by the projection—averages only 0.62%0.62\% across the full run, never exceeding ∼3.3%{\sim}3.3\%. AEGIS preserves the pre-trained VQA manifold by removing <1%<1\% of gradient energy on average, concentrated precisely in the destructive projection direction. This confirms that the cross-modal interference, while highly destructive in its cumulative effect, is geometrically thin: a narrow sliver of destructive energy that, left unchecked, accumulates into manifold-scale drift.

Near-orthogonality of task and anchor gradients.

The average cosine similarity between the task and OT gradients (Figure 5, bottom-left) fluctuates around zero (cos⁡θ¯≈0.008\bar{\cos\theta}\approx 0.008), indicating that the task and anchor gradients are nearly orthogonal on average. The destructive interference arises from the signed fluctuations around this mean—the momentary configurations where cos⁡θℓ\cos\theta_{\ell} dips negative. AEGIS captures exactly these transient destructive excursions while leaving the vast majority of gradient energy untouched.

Figure 6 provides a per-neuron view of the gradient conflict. The cosine-similarity distribution is heavily skewed toward negative values, confirming that at the neuron level, the flow-matching gradient predominantly
emphopposes the anchor-restoration gradient. This is the geometric signature of cross-modal interference that AEGIS is designed to eliminate.

7 Discussion and Conclusion

Mechanisms of preservation.

AEGIS successfully preserves the baseline VQA capabilities by strictly controlling the gradient geometry. We hypothesise two complementary mechanisms for this: (i) the orthogonal projection ensures that any novel spatial and geometric priors from the continuous robotic data are pushed into the orthogonal complement, enhancing rather than overwriting the existing knowledge manifold; (ii) the OT penalty acts as an implicit regulariser on the activation distribution, stabilising training dynamics and preventing the representational drift that typically accompanies aggressive fine-tuning.

LoRA’s failure mode.

Our LoRA baseline provides the controlled demonstration that LoRA fails to prevent VQA erosion during VLA fine-tuning. The failure is not due to insufficient rank (r=16r{=}16 provides ∼80{\sim}80M trainable parameters): it is geometric. LoRA constrains updates to a low-rank subspace span​(B)\text{span}(B), but this subspace is initialised randomly (Kaiming initialisation for BB, zeros for AA) and is not aligned with the VQA-critical parameter directions. The cross-modal MSE gradient, projected into this random subspace, retains its destructive component. AEGIS addresses the complementary dimension: it does not restrict where updates can occur (full rank) but restricts which direction updates may take (orthogonal to the anchor manifold’s normal). In principle, AEGIS and LoRA could be combined: LoRA restricts capacity while AEGIS restricts direction.

The geometry of near-orthogonality.

The average cosine similarity of ∼0.008{\sim}0.008 between task and OT gradients reveals that the FM gradient and anchor-restoration gradient occupy nearly perpendicular subspaces. This near-orthogonality is not coincidental: it reflects the fundamental independence of the action-prediction task (which requires learning new motor-control representations) and the VQA-preservation objective (which requires maintaining existing visual-linguistic representations). The two objectives are “nearly compatible” in gradient space—the destructive interference arises from signed fluctuations around this near-orthogonal mean, not from systematic opposition. This explains why AEGIS can preserve VQA while shedding only 0.62%0.62\% of gradient energy: the destructive component is genuinely small, but without correction, it accumulates over 1,5001{,}500 steps into the severe drift observed in naive FT.

Computational cost.

AEGIS adds a second backward pass per step (with graph retention for the first), approximately doubling backward-pass time. In practice, we observe ∼40%{\sim}40\% wall-clock overhead compared to naive FT, dominated by the retained computation graph. The static anchor is computed once (∼5{\sim}5 min) and reused. The per-step OGP computation (dot products, norms, and conditional subtraction) is O⁡(d)O(d) per layer and negligible compared to the backward passes.

Limitations.

While AEGIS resolves the cross-modal gradient asymmetry, it introduces additional computational overhead (a second backward pass and graph retention), although this increase remains substantially lower than the 2×2\times cost of mixed-batch co-training. Additionally, due to compute constraints for full-scale training runs, we do not evaluate closed-loop task success rates in simulation, focusing instead on the gradient and activation-level diagnostics that establish the mechanism of knowledge preservation.

Future directions.

Immediate extensions include: (i) scaling to full-training runs: validating that the preserved geometry translates to downstream task success in closed-loop simulation (RoboSuite (Zhu et al., 2020), Isaac Gym (Makoviychuk et al., 2021)) across 100100k+ steps; (ii) larger models: scaling to 7B+ VLMs and diverse robotic datasets (DROID (Khazatsky et al., 2024), Open X-Embodiment (Collaboration, 2024)) where the knowledge manifold is richer; (iii) online anchor updates: periodically refreshing the Wasserstein anchor from the current model to track the evolving activation landscape; (iv) adaptive projection: modulating the projection aggressiveness based on the running OT penalty magnitude, tightening protection as drift accumulates.

Conclusion.

We identified cross-modal gradient asymmetry—the fundamental geometric incompatibility between low-rank MSE gradients and CE-trained parameter landscapes—as the root cause of severe VQA erosion during VLA fine-tuning. We showed that LoRA, the industry-standard PEFT approach, fails to prevent this erosion because it constrains parameter capacity but not gradient geometry. We introduced AEGIS, a buffer-free, layer-wise orthogonal gradient projection framework that constructs a Wasserstein-22 Gaussian anchor over the pre-trained activation manifold and applies Gram–Schmidt orthogonalisation to eliminate destructive gradient interference. AEGIS achieves the best VQA preservation among methods enabling direct continuous learning (best VQA loss 0.3740.374, below the pre-trained baseline), while maintaining competitive flow-matching convergence—all without replay buffers, co-training data, or discrete proxy tokens. The framework sheds only 0.62%0.62\% of gradient energy on average, demonstrating that the destructive component of cross-modal gradients is small in magnitude but highly destructive when left uncorrected.

Appendix A VQA Evaluation Details

All conditions are evaluated on the same fixed 100100-sample subset of VQA v2 [Goyal et al., 2019] using a teacher-forced protocol: the model receives the image, question, and ground-truth answer tokens, and the cross-entropy loss on the answer tokens is computed. This loss-based evaluation provides a continuous, differentiable metric of VQA capability that is more sensitive than accuracy-based evaluation for detecting early-stage forgetting.

The evaluation prompt format is: answer en <image> {question}, with the ground-truth answer provided as a suffix. This format matches the PaliGemma2-3B-Mix-224 model’s native VQA evaluation protocol exactly. All experiments use 11-image evaluation format with max_length=512\texttt{max\_length}=512.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
